text.p: These are the leading stories in the Serbian and Montenegrin press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- SERBIA -
POLITIKA
- Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic promises members of the Belgrade university council members one month hand outs by May 1.
- UN administrator for Eastern Slavonia Jacques Klein said he would secure $300-400 million for reconstruction and return of displaced persons to their homes.
- Yugoslavia expects to sow some 1.4 million hectares under maize this spring and with a yield of five tonnes per hectare produce seven million tonnes of the crop.
- Serbian government has set a minimum wage at 200 dinars for the second quartal of the year.
- There are 1.36 million pupils and students in Serbia and the entire education system employs some 117.100 people.

- Yugoslavia to export 620 tonnes of dried plums at the value of $1 million to Russia by end of May in exchange for gas. The government plans exports of another 2.500 tonnes of dried plums from 1996 and this years crop at the value of some $4 million.
- Yugoslav government drafts a law on frozen hard currency savings estimated to stand at 6.7 billion German marks.
NASA BORBA
- Yugoslav deputy prime minister Danko Djunic expects European Union to approve trade preferentials to Yugoslavia at its meeting on April 29.
- Yugoslav chamber of commerce vice-president Momir Pavlicevic said EU preferentials could secure an increase of textile industry exports to half a billlion dollars.
- Serbian government deffers deadline for tax payments to revive economy and help financial consolidation of many firms.
- Serbia's health and social workers trade union threaten to call a nationwide strike unless members received their March pay by May 12.
- Cars with Yugoslav licence plates could be banned abroad because of accumulated debt of the insurance companies amounting to tens of millions German marks.
- Serbian government expected to adopt law on consessions on Wednesday to enable additional domestic investments and atract foreign funds.
VECERNJE NOVOSTI
- According to some estimates, there are at least 500 million dinars blocked in hard currency kept in "mattresses" in homes or in goods that do not have buyers.

- Owners of frozen hard currency accounts in Yugoslav banks and depositors of collapsed pyramid savings schemes call on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to arrest Dafiment bank owner Dafina Milanovic.

- Serbian Renewal Movement leader Vuk Draskovic says unless agreement on elections is reached by June 28 between the opposition coalition Zajedno and the Socialist Party of Serbia he will call people out for street protests.
- Zajedno opposition coaliton says it will return to the Serbian parliament after nearly two years if live television broadcasts are restored.
POLITIKA EKSPRES
- Serbian government decides to allow exchange of agricultural mechanisation for agricultural products.
- Heavy rain and snow halts spring sowing in the country, says Slavica Delevic of the Federal Hydrometeorology Institute.
- Croatia opens offices for registration of refugees in Vukovar, Beli Manastir, Ilok, Bilje, Tovarnik and Erdut, in Eastern Slavonia region. Return of refugees in both directions.
- UNTAES transitional administrator Jacques Klein verifies results of elections in Eastern Slavonia, Croatia.
- Moslem authorities in Serbia's Raska region boycotting the state.
- Public debate on privatisation law nears end. Fresh funds can be expected in second round.
-- MONTENEGRO --
POBJEDA

- There are no winners and no losers after the session of the main board of Montenegrin ruling Democratic Party of Socialists in a dispute between the republic's president Momir Bulatovic and prime minister Milo Djukanovic, says editorial.
- Montenegrin electric power company says electricity supply still unstable. Problem resolved by importing electricity from Greece, Bulgaria, Romania and Albania and electricity cuts.
- The upcoming visit of the International Monetary Fund technical mission to Belgrade in May might be crucial, paper writes in its commentary.
- Out of 6.500 teachers employed in elementary and 2.500 in secondary Montengrin schools half of them are on strike. They have reduced their classes to 30 from 45 minutes.
- April 25 and 28 and May 1 and 2 are non working days in Montenegro. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
